name: Model type detected from file name
answer:
EXPLICITLY, FROM A MANIFEST - not from the file name, and not from checkpoint metadata either. Both questions on the card get the same answer for the same reason.

SHOULD MODEL TYPE BE CHOSEN EXPLICITLY OR READ FROM CHECKPOINT METADATA? Explicitly, in a manifest that is written once when the checkpoint is mirrored and is then the only thing consulted. Checkpoint metadata sounds better than a file name and is still the wrong source: reading it means loading enough of a .pth to inspect it, which is an unpickle of an untrusted file (SEC-01), and a fine-tune saved by a third-party script may carry no such metadata or carry someone else's. A manifest entry is a statement by whoever put the file there, which is the only party that actually knows.

SHOULD MODEL SIZE COME FROM METADATA RATHER THAN FILE-NAME SUBSTRINGS? Same answer, same manifest, same line.

WHY THE FILE NAME CANNOT WORK, using the card's own cases. Legacy matches substrings, so:
  my_vit_l.pth              contains '_l.'  -> read as SAM 2 large -> fails to load at all
  sam2_hiera_large_tuned.pt contains '_t'   -> read as SAM 2 TINY  -> loads the wrong config
  database_v2.pth           contains 'base' -> read as SAM 1 vit_b -> loads as the wrong variant
The middle one is the instructive failure: it does not error. It builds a tiny config around large weights, and what the user gets is degraded output from a model they believe is their fine-tuned large. The card also records that the image and video predictors can pick DIFFERENT sizes from the same name, because they match different substring tables - so one checkpoint can be two different models depending on which code path reached it.

Underneath all of that is the design mistake rather than the bug: renaming a file changes how the software interprets its contents. A name is a place to find bytes, not a claim about what they are.

BUILT IN PHASE 2, at `modernized/lazylabel-reimagined/inference/src/lazylabel_inference/manifest.py`. Each entry declares name, family (sam1 or sam2), size, filename, sha256 and byte count; the parser refuses a family or size that is not valid for that family, a hash that is not 64 hex characters, a non-positive size, a duplicate model name, and a filename that is anything other than one plain path component. `tests/test_manifest.py::TestFileNameIsNotMeaning` runs all three of the card's misclassification cases and asserts the manifest reads them correctly, and asserts that renaming a checkpoint changes nothing about how it is interpreted.

A consequence worth stating: a checkpoint that is not in the manifest is not loadable. That is deliberate. Legacy searched recursively for .pth and .pt files and guessed at whatever it found, which is how an unrelated file in a subfolder became a model candidate. Adding a checkpoint is now an explicit act with a hash attached.
corrections: Rejected checkpoint metadata as the source as well as the file name: reading it requires unpickling an untrusted file (SEC-01), and a third-party fine-tune may not carry it.
Recorded that the worst case is the one that does NOT error - sam2_hiera_large_tuned.pt builds a tiny config around large weights and quietly degrades output.
Recorded the consequence of the manifest: a checkpoint not listed is not loadable, replacing legacy's recursive search-and-guess.
unresolved: How a user adds their own fine-tuned checkpoint in a hosted deployment, where they do not have shell access to edit a manifest. Phase 3 needs an upload path that computes the hash and appends an entry, or the feature is desktop-only. Not blocking the port - the manifest is right either way - but it is a capability legacy had and this design does not yet.
